slides.notes:
Hi, we are Team Cosmic Cats from Amman. Our challenge: identify Earth locations that are analogs of the permanent Moon base sites and of Mars.
Our goal: find where on Earth, and especially in Jordan, crews and rovers can rehearse before they fly. Analog Atlas is a 3D globe of Earth, the Moon and Mars that ranks 19 Earth sites against 13 Moon and Mars targets, using real, sourced data. If a value was not measured, the app says 'not measured'; we never invent a number.

items.text: NASA SPACE APPS CHALLENGE 2026 · AMMAN
ANALOG ATLAS
Find the Moon and Mars on Earth.
Goal: find the places on Earth, and in Jordan, where crews and rovers can rehearse for a Moon base or a Mars mission, using real, sourced data.
Challenge: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
Team Cosmic Cats

Mohammad Fathi Awni Ahmad · Ameer Hamam
Abdalrhman Ali Samih Alhaj Hassan · Moath Abu Aisha
App screenshot · Earth: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble (NASA GIBS)

slides.notes:
Each Earth site gets a score from four pillars: climate, terrain, geology and resources. The flat landing zone is shown next to it, but by default it does not change the score.
For the Moon base sites, climate also compares Sun height, how high the Sun gets in the sky, computed from latitude on both sides.
Climate, terrain and landing zone come from data: NASA POWER and MODIS on Earth, LRO on the Moon, NASA's orbiters and rovers on Mars, and elevation maps of all three worlds. Rock type and resources are sourced classifications: each one has a published source and an exact quote.
Where a value is a general figure and not a measurement at the site, the app labels it, and weak data gets a flag. If something was not measured, the app says 'not measured'. We never invent a number.
Satellites also show what the ground is made of: MODIS, Sentinel-2, ASTER and NASA's EMIT. The app shows it next to the score, but it never changes the score.

items.text: 01 · HOW WE SCORE
Four scored pillars, every value with its source.

items.title: Climate
items.body: Mean temperature, daily swing, coldest ground, rain and albedo. Moon base sites add Sun height.
items.source: NASA POWER 2001–2020 · MODIS · LRO Diviner · Mars Climate Sounder

items.title: Terrain
items.body: How steep the ground is in a 10 km box, on the same 500 m grid on all three worlds.
items.source: Copernicus DEM · LRO LOLA · MGS MOLA

items.title: Flat zone
items.body: Shown, not scored: the largest flat square with every slope under 10°, after NASA’s Artemis landing rule.

items.title: Geology
items.body: The main rock type: the same, related or different.

items.title: Resources
items.body: Water ice, caves for shelter, regolith to build with, salts and brines.
items.source: Every tag has a source and an exact quote

items.text: No guessing: a value that was not measured is shown as “not measured”, and weak data gets a ⚑ flag.
Also measured from orbit, shown but never scored: MODIS, Sentinel-2, ASTER and NASA EMIT show what the top of the ground is made of.

slides.notes:
Why these two places? We chose the two cave sites: the lava-tube pit in Mare Tranquillitatis on the Moon and the cave skylight on Arsia Mons on Mars. A lava tube shields a base from radiation, micrometeorites and the big temperature swing between day and night.
For both, the best Jordan twin is Harrat al-Shaam, the black basalt desert in north-east Jordan, with its own lava caves. For the Moon pit it is number one in the world, 71 percent. For the Mars skylight it scores 84 percent, one point behind Craters of the Moon in the USA, which is within the resolution of the data. One Jordanian lava field, two worlds. It also comes first for Jezero Crater and Apollo 11.
We also show where Jordan loses: for Gale, Phoenix and the ice-rich zones the best twins are in China and India. A score is not proof; it tells you where to test first.

slides.notes:
We put the base only where Jordan matches best: the two starred pairs. On the Moon, the lava-tube pit in Mare Tranquillitatis; on Mars, the cave skylight on Arsia Mons; both have Harrat al-Shaam as their Earth twin.
It is a concept, not an engineering design: two homes, a greenhouse, a communications room and solar power, joined by pressurised tunnels so nobody needs a spacesuit between rooms. The same base stands on Earth, where it is rehearsed, and on the Moon or Mars.
The hardest part is the people. On the space station astronauts sleep just over 6 hours a night. So the base has private bunks, a fixed routine, a greenhouse, and a room to talk to family: a message to Mars takes 3 to 22 minutes, so families send video messages.

items.text: 03 · THE BASE
A concept base where Jordan matches best.

Only the two ⭐ pairs get the base: the Moon’s Mare Tranquillitatis pit and Mars’ Arsia Mons skylight, both twinned with Harrat al-Shaam.
Two homes, a greenhouse, a communications room and solar power, joined by pressurised tunnels. The same base on Earth, the Moon and Mars.
Built for people

Private bunks and a fixed routine: astronauts on the space station sleep just over 6 hours a night.
A hydroponic greenhouse: potato, soybean and lettuce are the best low-cost set.
A message to Mars takes 3 to 22 minutes, so families send video messages.
Photo: Wadi Rum, Hansueli Krapf / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 (cropped, darkened, drawing added)

slides.notes:
The navigation problem. On Mars a command takes 3 to 22 minutes to arrive, so a rover cannot be driven live: it must judge slope and wheel slip by itself. That must be practised on Earth, on ground that has the same slopes.
Look at these two photos: one is the Moon, one is Iceland. Looking alike is not enough; the numbers must match.
The Jordan box near Wadi Rum has a median slope of 8.44 degrees over 1 kilometre, the Shackleton connecting ridge 8.56; over 2 kilometres, 7.91 and 7.67. From Copernicus and NASA LOLA elevation data. Nobody has checked it on the ground yet.
Our next step: a low-cost rover with the rocker-bogie suspension used on Mars since Sojourner, with a spectrometer, a soil probe, LiDAR and climate sensors on an ESP32. It drives the route, measures slip and energy per metre, and calibrates the satellite data. It is a concept; it is not built yet.

items.text: 04 · THE NAVIGATION PROBLEM
On the Moon and Mars, a rover drives alone.

A command to Mars takes 3 to 22 minutes, so a rover must judge slope and slip by itself.
That has to be rehearsed on Earth, on ground with the same slopes.
Our Jordan box near Wadi Rum: median slope 8.44° at 1 km; the Shackleton ridge: 8.56° (2 km: 7.91° vs 7.67°).
Next: drive a low-cost rocker-bogie rover there and measure slip and energy per metre. Concept, not built yet.
One is the Moon. One is Iceland.
